1:
Everyone feels the hinge. Henry begins with the melancholy conjunction that stops the pleasant prospect of the preceding chapters, since every church in its best state has its but: the disciples were holy, but there were hypocrites among them; selling their goods was their praise, but became a cloak for hypocrisy; and the signs so far had been miracles of mercy, but now comes a miracle of judgment, that God may be both loved and feared. Barnes sets the case against Barnabas, hypocrisy answering liberality, and defines the vice as the attempt to imitate whatever form religion has lately taken — here self-denial and benevolence. Calvin says the same in his own idiom: the company Luke described looked more like angels than men, and Satan, unable to prevail by open war, found a way inside under colour of that very virtue.

Who Ananias was is disputed. Gill notes the name is the same as Hananiah and signifies the grace of the Lord, warns that there is no dependence on names, and thinks he may have been a minister of the word, placed directly after Barnabas, perhaps one of the hundred and twenty — great gifts and no grace. Wesley denies him even that, since all who believed were of one heart, and supposes him unbaptized. Clarke leaves him in obscurity, remarking that his name agrees very ill with his conduct and his family is written in the dust. Lightfoot works instead on the transaction, asking whether Barnabas could have sold land inside Israel at all, and whether a Levite could hold land outside the cities of Levi, since the law allowed a man to part with his inheritance only under constraint of poverty — whereas here lands are sold for the poverty of others.

Where exactly the sin lay draws careful answers. Ellicott and Clarke clear the ground first: the money was his own and keeping it back no sin in itself, but selling in order to bring the price into the common stock left him no further claim, and offering the part as though it were the whole was an acted lie. Barnes adds that the sale could easily be known to the society while the price could not, which made the imposture possible, and that the word for the property does not say what kind it was. Henry divides the sin in three, ambition to pass for eminent disciples, a covetousness that would serve God and mammon at once, and the attempt to deceive the apostles, adding that it is of fatal consequence to carry profession further than the inward principle will bear. Calvin holds that Luke charges nothing but the feigned offering, then unpacks what was folded inside it — contempt of God, sacrilegious defrauding, vanity, unbelief — and recalls that Christ preferred the widow's two mites to the great sums of others.

The verb itself is worked over. Robertson parses it as a middle from a root meaning apart, to set aside for oneself; Barnes gives its ordinary use of a clandestine diversion of public money, and Ellicott adds that it always carries the idea of stealthy appropriation and stands in the Greek Old Testament for the sin of Achan. Gill says he reserved it after giving out that he sold the whole for the church; Wesley, that he brought it as if it were all. On the motive Robertson is blunt, that the praise of Joseph was too much for him and he wanted credit for giving all while taking care of himself; Calvin says the same more gravely, that a man ashamed not to be counted among the best will strip himself of part of his riches to buy a name, honouring the apostles' feet above the eyes of God. Lightfoot ends by asking how Ananias could think the Spirit deceivable, when Gehazi alone should have taught him how quick a prophet's discernment is.
3:
How Peter knew is answered the same way by all. Gill, Barnes and Calvin refer it to revelation, Gill comparing Elisha's knowledge of Gehazi and Calvin adding that the apostles here supply God's room; Ellicott calls it the prophetic gift by which he read the baseness under a show of devotion; Clarke names it the discernment of spirits, granted only at select times. Cyril presses the wonder rather than the mechanism — Peter was not there when they sold but was present by the Spirit, and with no accuser the unlettered fisherman learnt what the Greek sages never knew. Lightfoot asks whether the authority to sentence came from the commission about retaining sins or from immediate revelation, and observes what nobody else does: the man who denied his Master with a lie is the one who executes another for lying.

On Satan's part the comment leaves the guilt where it belongs. Clarke reports that the verb rendered fill means rather instigate, and argues that Peter would never have spoken so if no such agency existed. Barnes traces great crimes to the father of lies but insists the sin lay in yielding, since temptation nowhere excuses. Ellicott hears in the question why a proof that resistance was possible, and compares the sin of Judas for its malignant subtlety, a perversion of will just as it seemed about to reach a higher perfection. Robertson notices that the verb is the one used of being filled with the Holy Spirit, and says flatly that the devil filled his heart and Ananias did it too; Calvin distinguishes the pricks of Satan, which every man feels, from Satan's reigning in the whole man, which he calls the sign of a reprobate.

What the lying governs divides the two most careful readers. Ellicott sets out both possibilities, an offence against the Spirit dwelling in the Apostles or against the Spirit as searcher of his own heart, and though the parallel a verse later favours the first, he lets the deliberate change of case tip him toward the second — an accusative here, a dative there. Calvin weighs the same alternatives and comes down the other way on the same kind of evidence, since the Greek verb takes a double accusative; Robertson notes the difference of case without pressing it. Barnes, Clarke, Wesley and Calvin use the parallel for a doctrinal end, since lying to the Spirit is called lying to God, and Barnes argues at length that sin cannot be committed against an attribute but only against a person. Ellicott grants the inference and its limits, that the Apostles thought the Spirit sent by the Father and so distinct, yet did not shrink from calling him God.

That the sale was voluntary is unanimous, and pressed as the aggravation. Gill, Barnes, Wesley and Calvin all note that Ananias need never have sold, nor brought the money after selling; Calvin turns it into a rebuke of those who say the faithful may own nothing, and reminds the hypocrite that where two or three are gathered Christ presides. Ellicott puts it most exactly: he wanted the reputation of saintliness without the reality of sacrifice, and so incurred sacrilege without a consecration and perjury without an oath. On the death the note is cautious. Barnes calls it God's judgment and not Peter's act, while allowing natural means; Robertson says it is needless to blame Peter; Ellicott observes that Peter pronounced no formal sentence, and refuses to speculate beyond the visible judgment. Calvin defends the apostle positively, comparing Elymas struck blind, and answers two objections: those who call it cruel weigh the sin in their own balance and not God's, and those who think it slight because hypocrites escape daily miss that God showed in two what awaits all. Wesley adds that the severity was also wise, deterring imitators and proving the apostles' integrity with the money entrusted to them.
7:
The interval is read as mercy. Wesley calls it a precious space, the woman having longer for repentance; Calvin says providence separated the two so that the Church might see each betray a wickedness of its own, and adds the point that clinches it — Sapphira was not shamed into the lie by seeing her husband tell it, so not even bashfulness can be pleaded. Gill accounts for the three hours practically, since Jewish burying-places lay above a mile and a half outside the city. Robertson renders it an interval of about three hours; Barnes says only that her equal guilt drew the same judgment.

Peter's question is taken by two of them as a last offer. Ellicott supposes she came to ask why her husband had not returned, and observes that the question opened a way of repentance: she might once have saved him by a word of protest and might now have cleared herself by confession, missing the second chance as she had misused the first. Calvin makes it a rule of divine procedure, that God does not strike at once but tries the matter through, so vengeance falls only on the obstinate; the question is a calm invitation, and by holding carelessly on she showed herself incurable. Barnes turns to the form of the lie, since the sum named was true as far as it went and the deception lay in the suppression, a commoner species of falsehood than an open lie.

On the tempting the accounts converge. Barnes and Ellicott both take it as a trial of whether the Spirit in the Apostles could discern the secrets of hearts. Calvin defines the offence from Scripture usage, that God is tempted when his power is taken from him or his knowledge denied, and finds it monstrous that two should make their match with God shut out. Robertson judges the act close to the unpardonable sin of ascribing the manifest work of the Spirit to Beelzebub. Gill says only that for man and wife to agree in a fraud is dreadful. Cyril reaches the same ground by way of Gehazi, whose master asked whether his heart had not gone with him, shut in by the body yet seeing afar off, and concludes that the Spirit not merely rids of ignorance but invests with knowledge. Ellicott adds that the sentence is announced before it falls, and that to her shame was added the thought that her husband's death was in some sense her doing.

Clarke alone asks what became of them. The death, he insists, came neither from Peter's words nor from shame but by an immediate judgment of God, and theirs was a sin unto death in the strict sense, the body punished while mercy was extended to the soul; but the case cannot become a precedent, those who have seen such severity having more to fear if they presume upon mercy. The word for the assembly draws the closest notice. Ellicott marks it as the first occurrence since our Lord's two anticipatory uses, traces it through the Greek Old Testament and the civic assemblies of Greece, and suspects it marks the growth of the Hellenistic element; Robertson observes that the sense of a gathering is already fading, and that it was by now dangerous to follow Christ unless one walked straight. Clarke and Wesley give the same fivefold description of a New Testament church, called by the Gospel, grafted in by baptism, animated by love, united by fellowship, and disciplined by this judgment. Calvin separates two fears, that of the faithful, whom God's judgments always teach more, and that of outsiders, which fell short of worship though it made them give God the glory; Barnes turns the case on his readers, asking how many who profess to have devoted all to God would spend millions on themselves and not a penny for tribute.
12:
Henry marks the turn of the current: many miracles of mercy for one of judgment, God having come out of his place to punish and now returning to the mercy-seat, the signs done not in a corner but among a people free to examine them. Calvin says the same, that these works are more proper to the gospel because they show goodness as well as power, and that miracles serve faith, which is why they must never be separated from the word. On the meeting-place Barnes finds two purposes, worship at the regular hours and preaching to the crowds; Ellicott, dating the scene some months after Pentecost, puts it in winter, when that eastward portico caught the morning sun. Henry wonders that the rulers tolerated the meetings at all, and adds that there was no murmuring over the death of Ananias, as there had been against Moses after Korah. Calvin turns the unanimity into an argument for assembly, a Church where each man is his own teacher being bound to decay.

Who the rest were is open. Lightfoot confines them to the hundred and twenty, Ananias perhaps among them, so terrified by the fate of one of their order that they dared not claim equality with the Twelve. Barnes calls that far-fetched and prefers the rich and the men of authority, chiefly on the contrast drawn with the common people and the earlier cases of rulers who believed but feared to confess. Ellicott takes it for the Pharisees who sympathised without the courage to attach themselves; Clarke follows Calmet in making them the sects, none of which dared join a body that had adopted none of their opinions; Gill settles on men inside the church, ministers included; Wesley cuts it short, that no formalist dared join in outward show. Calvin treats the fear itself as the second fruit of the miracles and turns the point on his own age — there is a secret majesty in holy discipline which binds even the wicked, but we have made ourselves despised along with the gospel by our profane liberty of living.

The increase is read as a consequence, not a survival. Wesley says true believers were the more added because unbelievers kept their distance; Robertson notes the tense, that they kept on being added where one might expect a decrease. Barnes draws the rule that purging a church of unworthy members increases both its numbers and its purity, since men will not trouble to enter a body that does not care to be pure. Henry and Ellicott both stop at the women, Henry noting how much less notice the Jewish church took of them, Ellicott that the mention prepares for the dispute about the widows.

The shadow divides them. Barnes is careful: the writer neither says anyone was healed so, nor that they were told to try it, but records only what the people believed might happen, the express statement about Paul's handkerchiefs standing in contrast. Henry thinks it plainly succeeded, like the touch of Christ's hem, and finds the promise of greater works fulfilled in it — while denying that any virtue can be inferred for the relics of dead saints, since not one cure is recorded from Christ's own. Lightfoot asks the question none of the others ask, why Peter's shadow rather than another's, and answers twice: the sick were carried out only when he was known to be passing, and those who carried them may have known no other by sight. Barnes distinguishes the soft beds of the rich from the pallets of the poor, and guesses the sun near setting. Gill has the sick brought out into every street; Cyril sums the scene as it struck him, that men so gentle became objects of dread, the streets filling with beds and the towns round about sending their sick, all healed in the power of the Holy Ghost.
17:
Barnes and Robertson both defuse the word rendered sect, the root of our heresy but carrying no reproach in the New Testament and meaning only a party; Clarke agrees, and turns it into a long protest against the Roman use of the term. Ellicott passes over the word for the fact, recorded distinctly only here: that the high priests were Sadducees explains their whole course, while the Pharisees drifted from neutrality to open adherence. Barnes makes it sharper — one sect will watch the growth of another it hates, if that growth humbles a rival — and traces the enmity to the preaching of the resurrection, which overthrew the Sadducean position. Henry says that men of no religion are often bitterest against true religion, and that no good work went forward without opposition; Calvin reads the outbreak as blind fury, so little checked by evident divine power that it should teach the rest of us to submit betimes.

The prison and the release are read as sign, not rescue. Ellicott hears severity in the word public, the apostles being herded with robbers, and Robertson adds that any prison is bad enough. On the angel Ellicott insists the narrative is plainly supernatural, notes that those who want the history without the miracle must suppose some bold disciple mistaken for an angel in the dark, and answers the sneer that a deliverance ending in re-arrest served no purpose: the sign told on the Council and on the apostles' courage, and release even for a few hours from that company was no small boon. Calvin warns against expecting more, since the Lord did not free them from their enemies at all — they were beaten with rods soon after — but showed only that their life was defended so far as was expedient; and he lingers on the dignity of the means, the noblest creatures being set to watch over our safety.

Chrysostom alone asks why it was done at night, and answers from the pattern of Christ's own miracles: men were never shown the thing in the act, only the proofs — the Resurrection unseen, the water turned to wine unnoticed by drinkers already full. So here the apostles are not seen coming out, but the shut doors and posted guards are, a twofold security like the seal and the watch at the sepulchre; and, like Nebuchadnezzar seeing the three praising God in the furnace, the onlookers are convinced by what remains. He adds the sharpest note, that the rulers' first question ought to have been how the men got out, and instead they ask whether they had not been charged to be silent.

The angel's phrase draws four readings. Lightfoot finds no difficulty once the Sadducees are remembered: the words of this life are those that assert this life, the resurrection they deny, which was the whole controversy. Robertson agrees; Ellicott makes it the eternal life that consists in knowing God, in which the angels are sharers; Calvin takes the demonstrative for a gesture of certainty, as though the angel pointed at life with his finger; Wesley glosses it as the words that show the way to life everlasting. On the errand Gill, Barnes and Calvin agree that the release was not for safety: Barnes puts it that God sometimes delivers us from danger that we may plunge into new dangers, Calvin that many who escape persecution fall silent as though their duty were done, whereas these knew they were to live and die to the Lord. Of the morning Robertson notes that the temple doors stood open early, and he, Ellicott and Barnes all take the senate for elders distinct from the council, assessors called in for age and experience — though Clarke confesses that how they differed is past knowing.
22:
The report is treated as evidence. Barnes points out that the prison had not been broken open, that the guards were still keeping watch as if nothing had happened, and that the officers held the only means of entry, so that the deliverance could not have been human. Clarke lingers on the astonishment of men who had themselves shut the apostles up, found every bolt as they left it, and opened to find nobody within. Robertson glosses their title as under-rowers, the servants who executed the Sanhedrin's orders, and calls the sentinels before the doors a graphic picture; Gill piles up the fastenings, locked and barred and bolted. Wesley alone accounts for the state of the place with a guess, that the angel had probably shut the doors again behind him.

What the rulers made of it divides them. Barnes says the proof was clear and they need not have doubted, adding that sinners are simply not disposed to be convinced; he glosses the verb from the state of a man who has lost his way, and lists what had gone wrong for them — their authority disregarded, God opposing them by a miracle, the doctrine gaining ground, every effort against it wasted. Clarke leaves them genuinely undecided whether the escape was magic or a real miracle. Ellicott thinks they did not recognise anything supernatural and probably supposed human help; he also prefers the reading high priest to the bare priest, which has no parallel in the New Testament, and identifies the captain as commander of the Levite sentinels. Robertson makes the perplexity continuous and reads the grammar as a question about what the thing would come to if allowed to go on — then adds his flourish, that they little knew how that grain of mustard seed would outgrow every tree, and how dwarfed the tree of Judaism would look beside it. Wesley says only that they were at their wits' end, and that the world, in persecuting the children of God, entangles itself in numberless difficulties.

Of the informer Gill guesses nothing but his motive, holding it hardly possible that a disciple brought the news and likelier that an enemy came officiously to earn the favour of the chief priests; Clarke has the message arrive while the council sat baffled, that the men imprisoned the night before were teaching in the temple. On the arrest itself the comment turns admiring. Henry notices that they were not pulled from the pulpit nor bound nor dragged, and suggests the officers may have feared to be struck like Ananias or scorched as the mockers of Elias were — though he concludes that nothing restrained them but fear of the people. Robertson reads the imperfect as a slow and solemn leading, and puts the fear plainly, that they handled the apostles gently lest they be stoned. Barnes and Ellicott turn the moment on the apostles instead: Ellicott notes that they set the example of unresisting acquiescence when the tide of popular feeling would easily have carried a tumult, and Barnes that a summons was enough because they never meant to refuse an answer, and that going before the council gave them another opportunity to bear witness. Clarke supposes the officers had to entreat rather than command, the apostles going cheerfully as holding it their duty to obey every ordinance of man for the Lord's sake. Henry answers the obvious question, why they were freed at night only to be taken in the morning, by saying it humbled their persecutors and proved the discharge no flight from trial — and remarks that the powers which should have been a terror to evil works had become one to the good.
27:
The high priest's charge is read as two charges, and the second betrays him. Calvin separates them: contumacy, for disobeying the decree, and a private grievance dressed as public, since what nettles the priests is fear of being called to account for a murder. Wesley makes it blunter, that the enemies of the Gospel frame interdicts which the obedient cannot but break and then punish the innocent as guilty, and calls the complaint about the blood an artful and invidious word. Ellicott hears both scorn and fear in the careful avoidance of the name, and finds it a strange complaint from men who had stirred the crowd to cry that his blood be on them; Robertson calls the phrase this man a contemptuous slur, noting the same refusal to name Jesus in later rabbinic writing. Barnes turns the accusation into a compliment, since it is well if the only charge an enemy can bring is zeal in spreading the religion, and observes that the apostles never pressed the charge of murder except in the rulers' own hearing — their consciences supplied the rest.

The answer is the same as before, and everyone notices that it is. Barnes and Clarke refer it back to the earlier hearing, Clarke adding that the commission had come from God and could not be laid down at men's command; Robertson says moral necessity left them no choice; Ellicott observes that the angel's order in the night had given the old principle new force. Calvin states the rule and its limits: the comparison between God and man arises only where there is contrariety, and where authority is lawfully used it is out of season, since God chooses to be heard through men. But the moment rulers lead us away from obedience their titles vanish — a father not content with his own estate is only a man, and so is a king or a pastor who goes beyond his office.

The counter-charge is pressed without softening. Barnes says Peter took no pains to mitigate it, the mention of the killing identifying the person raised and confirming a death the rulers had themselves verified. Ellicott and Robertson both trace the phrase about the tree to the Greek of Deuteronomy and the curse on one hanged; Robertson glosses the verb for slew as laying violent hands on. Gill takes the raising up not of the resurrection but of the calling of Christ to the work of a Saviour, while Barnes and Clarke refer it to the resurrection. Gill and Clarke both observe that by naming the God of the fathers the apostles show they preach no strange God, but the very Saviour the fathers looked for.

On the exaltation Gill, Calvin and Robertson agree that the phrase means by his power rather than to a place at his side, Calvin adding that this is set against every enterprise of Satan, which can never climb high enough to hinder the hand of God. Ellicott notes that the word is the one the fourth Gospel applies to the lifting up on the cross. Of the two titles Barnes says the prince is actually exercising the office, and Clarke that Saviour and Jesus are nearly the same word; Calvin binds them together, that Christ is set in the highest honour to govern his people and to be the author of their salvation, the sum of the gospel lying in the repentance and remission that follow. Barnes asks how an exalted Christ can give repentance and answers four ways, chiefly that his acceptance made forgiveness possible and that his exaltation brought the Spirit. Clarke turns it pastoral: if such men as stood before the apostles could be saved, none need despair. Cyril adds only the frame, the Twelve cast into prison, delivered by night, standing again in the judgment hall.
33:
The verb is a saw for all four who parse it. Barnes says wrath seized the mind as a saw does wood, Clarke that they were sawn through and stung not with remorse but with spite. Ellicott and Robertson both press the contrast with the earlier scene, where men pricked to the heart repented, whereas this lacerating pain led only to hatred; Robertson adds that it is rage cutting into them here, not conviction of sin. Calvin alone finds a positive force even in this. The priests ought to have been moved though their hearts were iron, and instead they burst — whence he gathers that no argument brings the reprobate to obey unless God speaks within; yet the word pierces them all the same and urges their consciences, their fury springing from the sense of being arraigned by their judge, since there is a hidden majesty in the gospel which scatters all their ease. Robertson says they were plotting to kill on the spot and quotes the verdict that they were on the point of a grave judicial blunder, disobedience to the Sanhedrin being no capital offence; Barnes thinks their minds were made up but doubts any formal decree was passed, and adds that gospel doctrine often has just this effect.

Gamaliel is identified in almost the same words by three of them, since Barnes and Clarke both take their account from Lightfoot: Rabban Gamaliel the elder, president of the council after his father Simeon, Paul's master, the thirty-fifth receiver of the traditions and therefore a doctor of the law, dead eighteen years before the fall of Jerusalem, his son Simeon succeeding him and perishing in the ruins of the city. Ellicott fills in the ancestry instead, making him grandson of Hillel, the tolerant rival of the narrow and fanatical Shammai, whose precepts recall the Sermon on the Mount, and notes that the office passed through four generations, so that there seemed likely to be a dynasty of scribes. Barnes adds the party detail that matters, that the men most active against the apostles were Sadducees, while the Pharisees stood with them on the very doctrine at issue; Wesley notes that a Pharisee believed the resurrection, and that God can raise defenders of his servants whenever he pleases; Gill notes only the custom that a member who wished to speak rose from his seat.

How far he leaned toward the new faith is the one real dispute. Chrysostom cannot believe that a man so right-minded and so learned in the law persisted in unbelief to the end, and reads his intervention as evidence. Lightfoot answers the hope directly: he died a Pharisee, and he approved, if he did not write, the prayer composed against the heretics. Barnes says there is not the least evidence that he was a friend of the Christian religion, only that he was a man of far more liberal views than the rest of the council, and Clarke agrees that he probably favoured it not at all, while calling the advice he was about to give humane, sensible, candid and enlightened. Chrysostom alone examines how the speech was built. Gamaliel puts the council in fear at the outset, addresses them as though he shared their opinion so as not to be suspected of taking the prisoners' part, and uses no vehemence, speaking as to men drunk with passion; he warns them to take heed before producing his examples, and declares his own opinion only after they are cited. Barnes explains the clearing of the room on the usual grounds, that the accused were customarily made to withdraw while the council deliberated. Henry sees a hand behind the intervention, that the Lord still has all hearts in his keeping and sometimes directs the prudence of the worldly wise so as to restrain persecutors.
36:
Theudas is the crux, and the answers are five. All report that Josephus places a rising under a Theudas in the reign of Claudius, ten years or more after Gamaliel spoke. Lightfoot supposes Josephus has slipped in his chronology, and remarks that those who postulate a second Theudas merely imagine one without naming him. Barnes refuses the premise, denying that the two passages need refer to the same man: the name was common, Luke is as credible as Josephus, and Josephus reports the country as swarming with such disorders without professing to record them all. Clarke reports Pearce's conjecture that Luke's Theudas is the Judas who rebelled in Galilee just after Herod's death, Theudas and Thaddeus and Judas being interchangeable names, then declines to pursue it. Ellicott gives the fullest defence, granting that critics have made the passage proof of a portentous blunder and answering point by point — the numbers differ, Josephus speaking of a very great multitude and Gamaliel of about four hundred; Josephus records three risings just after Herod's death and many nameless pretenders besides; and a writer of Luke's culture in Nero's reign could hardly have inverted the order, any more than a Tudor historian would have put Wat Tyler after Jack Cade. Robertson leaves it open, noting that Josephus tells of four men named Simon in forty years and three named Judas in ten, so that one must decide which historian to credit; Calvin cuts the knot differently, holding that Gamaliel is not narrating in order but setting two like examples side by side without regard to time.

Calvin alone thinks the examples badly chosen. Judas was not resisted at once, so his sedition cost many lives before he was put down, and Theudas would have done far more harm had Fadus not scattered him in time; Gamaliel's whole point is that men who advance themselves rashly come to nothing, and if the priests will not hear God they deserve to be left wavering after a man's frivolous arguments. Gill and Barnes both note the boast of being somebody, which Barnes takes for a claim to be a prophet or the Messiah; Robertson marks the dispersal as a decisive going to pieces.

The advice is admired and distrusted at once. Robertson sums the policy as hands off; Barnes puts the dilemma plainly, that a human plan will collapse of itself as the other two did, and a divine one cannot be overthrown. Ellicott turns cooler: the advice implies a suppressed conviction not bold enough to utter itself, and places Gamaliel among the perennial waiters upon Providence, neutral until a cause succeeds and then coming forward with tardy sympathy. Wesley marks the limits: a manifestly good cause should be joined at once, a manifestly evil one opposed at once, and the advice is useful only in a sudden and doubtful case; he adds that Gamaliel corrects himself, calling it a work rather than a counsel, truer than he knew. Clarke adds that whatever pretends to be done in God's name but is not of him will have his curse.

Barnes alone builds the second horn into an argument. He observes that Gamaliel plainly allowed the thing might be divine, showing a more candid mind than the rest of the council, and turns the test forward: opposing error harshly is the surest way to fix men in it, error left alone commonly dies of itself, and the Christian religion has stood too long to be of men, having outlasted systems sustained by the sword and by the state. He presses the closing word as hard, to fight against God being the most fearful posture a man can take. Ellicott adds a note of translation, preferring overthrown so that the same verb may stand in both halves of the dilemma; Gill defines the other half as a work formed after the counsel of God's will.
40:
The council took half the advice, and everyone says so. Barnes explains that they abandoned the design of killing but would not let the apostles alone, since releasing them unpunished would look like a defeat — whence his remark that men who cannot accomplish their full malignity will take up some petty annoyance rather than let it alone. Ellicott reads the vote by parties: the Sadducees would have preferred violence, the Pharisees were strong enough to carry a middle course, and the scourging was the priests' price for it; he notes too that this is the first persecution to fall on the whole Twelve, and reads the sentence forensically, a conviction on the lesser charge of disturbing the Temple with a verdict of not proven on the graver charge of heresy. Robertson calls the outcome a draw, with Gamaliel the tactical victor: the Sanhedrin stood by their guns but refused to shoot. Clarke locates the fear precisely, that it was Jesus and not the apostles the council feared, since if the doctrine were preached it must prevail and they must come to nothing — which he matches with the Marian bishops who said that if they did not put down printing it would put them down.

Calvin alone refuses to admire the compromise. He notes how great the rage still was, and gives the verdict that doubtful counsels in which men alone are considered and God's truth set aside come to no good: Gamaliel gets the lives spared, while the Son of God is slandered in their persons and the gospel buried in silence so far as its enemies can manage. He turns this on his readers, since many think they have obeyed God well enough if they save the lives of men in danger for the gospel, while not fearing to press them into a denial of Christ, whose confession is more precious in God's sight than the lives of all men.

The rejoicing is felt as the reversal of the whole scene. Barnes observes that nothing seems more disgraceful than a public whipping, that the rulers meant the shame to keep the apostles out of public view, and that the effect was the reverse; he gives six reasons for the joy, then one careful restriction, that the words say the council judged them fit to suffer shame, not that God esteemed them worthy. Ellicott and Clarke both take it the other way. Ellicott hears the beatitude behind it, the Twelve feeling for the first time that they could rejoice and be exceeding glad as the prophets before them; Clarke claims the temper as a New Testament privilege, since the choicest saints of the older dispensation fretted or mourned or at best possessed their souls in patience, whereas Christians exulted; and Wesley calls joy in affliction a sure mark of the truth.

The close is read as a triumph rather than a survival. Robertson notes that they went back to the very place of the arrest, and calls it a great day for the disciples; he identifies the two participles as teaching and evangelising, with Jesus as object and the Christ as predicate, so that the substance of the earliest preaching was that Jesus of Nazareth is the promised Messiah. Ellicott supposes the captain of the Temple now let the movement run uninterrupted. Gill has them at it daily, publicly and privately; Clarke turns it into a charge to preachers, that men who loved their Master, his work and their thankless countrymen, and hated nothing but their own lives, were the proper persons to convert the world. Calvin adds the note that joins the two halves, that constancy accompanied the joy, since no man faints who reckons himself happy in suffering for Christ — so the apostles were armed by their stripes, while we, having borne a little persecution, resign the torch as though we were worn-out soldiers.
